title: Designing the perfect assessment system, part 2
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou continues her series on national assessment design by tackling the common claim that formative assessment should take priority over the other purposes. She argues that good formative assessment is highly specific, giving students precise next steps, and that a national system built around it would need an equally specific national curriculum. Such detail, down to what happens when students confuse two characters or leave zero out of a mean, is very hard for central government to mandate. She weighs the counterexample of 1970s Finland, whose prescriptive centralised curriculum succeeded, but judges it unsuited to a system the size of England. Her conclusion is that governments should concentrate on reliable summative scores and accountability and leave formative practice to schools, while avoiding vague progression-statement banks that are prescriptive without being specific.
points: Formative assessment is only as useful as it is specific, so prioritising it nationally would require a far more detailed national curriculum than England has.
Government may do better setting rules and incentives than dictating classroom detail, which means leaving formative assessment to practitioners.
Finland shows centralised, prescriptive curricula can work, but system size and scale make it a poor model for England.
The worst option is the adverb soup of generic progression statements, which Christodoulou calls prescriptive without being specific.
quotes: The problem with this argument is that good formative assessment is very specific - it aims to give students precise next steps on what they need to do next to improve. A national system that prioritised formative assessment would therefore also require a very specific national curriculum - far more so than the one we have at the moment.

I mean guidance on what happens when you are teaching An Inspector Calls and students mix up Eric and Gerald, or what happens when students calculate the mean of a set of numbers and don’t include 0. This level of specific detail is what students need to improve and overcome misconceptions, but this level of specific detail is also very hard for central government to mandate.

Finland, for example, reformed its education system in the 1970s in an extremely prescriptive fashion, and it rose to the top on international tests. Here’s a quotation from Amanda Ripley’s The Smartest Kids in the World explaining how it worked.

I don’t think an approach like this would work in England in 2024 for a number of reasons, one of which is the size of the system. England has a population of about 60 million, and about 20,000 schools, 4,000 of which are secondaries.

Whatever approach a government chooses, one thing it has to avoid is recommending an “adverb soup” approach to formative assessment, where teachers are given banks of statements like “Can use vocabulary creatively and originally” and encouraged to use them to provide students with formative feedback. I’ve called this the tyranny of the progression statement. It’s the worst of both worlds: prescriptive without being specific.
